subject: VAPA
overview: VAPA 7 rotates through drawing, color and painting, music literacy and performance, printmaking across cultures, theatre, media arts and sculpture, ending in a family exhibition. Each week follows a create–present–respond–connect rhythm: look at a master work, practice a technique, make a piece, then reflect in the sketchbook. Praise effort and specific choices rather than 'talent,' date every sketchbook page so growth is visible, and keep finished work flat and labeled for the portfolio in weeks 34–36.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, pencils (2H, HB, 2B, 4B, 6B), a fine felt-tip pen, a shoe, a timer. Draw a few blind contours yourself so you can model laughing at the wobbly results.
misconceptions: Thinking blind contour drawings should look 'right.' The goal is training eye–hand coordination and careful looking; distorted results are expected.
Using one uniform line everywhere. Vary line weight: heavier for edges in shadow or nearer, lighter for distant or lit edges.

days.guide: Your child designs a cover and fills a page with 20 line types; label a few (contour, gestural, implied, hatched).

questions.q: What is line quality?
questions.a: The character of a line — its thickness, darkness, smoothness or roughness, and how it varies.

days.guide: Explain blind contour: eyes on the hand, never on the paper, pencil moving slowly as eyes trace edges. Three 3-minute drawings.

questions.q: What is a contour line?
questions.a: A line that follows the edges (outer and inner) of a form.

questions.q: Why draw without looking at the paper?
questions.a: It forces you to really observe the object and trains eye–hand coordination.

days.guide: Modified contour: look mostly at the shoe, glance at the paper only at corners or turns. Include laces, stitching and inner edges.

questions.q: How is modified contour different from blind contour?
questions.a: You can glance at the paper occasionally (at key points) to keep proportions, while still looking mostly at the object.

days.guide: Try three idea starters: draw a random object, a word prompt, and one object 5 different ways.

questions.q: Name one strategy to beat creative block.
questions.a: Use a prompt, change the medium, set a timer, draw one object many ways, or look at artists for inspiration.

days.guide: Your child picks the best contour and writes three sentences about line quality.

questions.q: Point to a place where you varied line weight. Why?
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., darker line where the shoe touches the floor to show weight and shadow.

weeks.assessment_key: Sketchbook rubric (1–4): cover design shows personal identity; line page has 20 distinct line types (thick, thin, dashed, zigzag, spiral, wavy, broken, implied, hatched, etc.); three blind contours of 3 minutes each with continuous line; modified contour shoe with accurate shapes and varied line; idea-starter page full. Reflection proficient: three sentences using 'line quality' vocabulary (weight, continuity, expressiveness) about a specific drawing.

weeks.prep: Pencils 2H–6B, a blending stump or tissue, an egg and a ball, a desk lamp (single strong light from one side). Find a Renaissance drawing (e.g., a Leonardo or Dürer study) online.
misconceptions: Outlining shapes with a dark line and filling in. Real objects have edges defined by value changes, not outlines.
Forgetting reflected light, making shadows flat. Light bounces off the table into the shadow side, so it's slightly lighter near the bottom edge.

days.guide: Make a 9-step pencil value scale (light pressure/2H to heavy/6B), then a hatching and cross-hatching scale.

questions.q: What is value?
questions.a: How light or dark a color or tone is.

questions.q: How does cross-hatching make a darker value?
questions.a: Layers of crossing lines placed closer together cover more paper.

days.guide: Draw three spheres and shade with highlight, midtone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.

questions.q: Put these in order from lightest to darkest on a sphere: core shadow, highlight, reflected light, midtone.
questions.a: Highlight, midtone, reflected light, core shadow (the core shadow is darkest on the object; cast shadow nearest the object is darkest overall).

questions.q: Which direction does the cast shadow fall?
questions.a: Away from the light source.

days.guide: Set up the egg under the lamp; 25-minute realistic study, building value gradually.

questions.q: Why start shading lightly?
questions.a: You can always darken, but heavy graphite is hard to erase.

days.guide: Shade a crumpled paper bag using different pencil grades for sharp folds and soft planes.

questions.q: Which pencil is softer and darker: 2H or 6B?
questions.a: 6B (B pencils are softer/darker; H pencils are harder/lighter).

days.guide: Compare the egg to a Renaissance drawing (e.g., Leonardo's studies, which use hatching and soft modeling called sfumato).

questions.q: What technique did Leonardo use for soft transitions between light and shadow?
questions.a: Sfumato (smoky, gradual blending); he also used hatching in drawings.

weeks.assessment_key: Value scale: 9 even steps from white to black with no jumps; hatching/cross-hatching scale also shows 9 steps. Egg study rubric (1–4): accurate oval shape, full value range, highlight, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow placed correctly for the light source, smooth gradation, no outline. Proficient = all 4 shadow parts present and consistent with the lamp.

weeks.prep: Ruler, pencil, eraser, print or screen image of Raphael's The School of Athens (1509–1511, Vatican). Try a one-point box yourself first.
misconceptions: Placing the horizon line at the top of the page by default. The horizon line is eye level; it changes depending on where the viewer stands.
Drawing vertical lines toward the vanishing point. In one- and two-point perspective, vertical edges stay vertical; only receding edges go to vanishing points.

days.guide: Draw a horizon line and one vanishing point; draw initials as flat block letters, then connect corners to the VP to make them 3-D.

questions.q: What is a vanishing point?
questions.a: The point on the horizon line where parallel receding lines appear to meet.

questions.q: What does the horizon line represent?
questions.a: The viewer's eye level.

days.guide: Trace the floor tiles and architecture lines in The School of Athens until they meet.

questions.q: Where is the vanishing point in The School of Athens?
questions.a: At the center, near Plato and Aristotle, the two central figures — drawing the viewer's eye to them.

days.guide: Draw a room or hallway in one-point: back wall rectangle, orthogonals from its corners to the edges, add doors and furniture.

questions.q: What are orthogonals?
questions.a: Diagonal lines that recede toward the vanishing point.

days.guide: Two-point: horizon line with VPs near the page edges; draw the nearest vertical building edge, connect top and bottom to both VPs.

questions.q: When do you use two-point perspective?
questions.a: When you view an object from a corner, so two sides recede to two vanishing points.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph on perspective in the Renaissance.

questions.q: Who is credited with first demonstrating linear perspective?
questions.a: Filippo Brunelleschi, in Florence in the early 1400s (Leon Battista Alberti later explained it in writing).

weeks.assessment_key: Perspective drawings rubric (1–4): horizon line and vanishing point(s) clearly marked; all receding lines (orthogonals) converge accurately; verticals vertical and horizontals horizontal (one-point); objects shrink with distance; neat ruler work. Reflection proficient: explains that Renaissance artists (Brunelleschi demonstrated it ~1415–20; Alberti wrote it up in 1435) used linear perspective to create the illusion of 3-D depth on a flat surface, making scenes look realistic and drawing the eye to a focal point (e.g., Plato and Aristotle in The School of Athens).

weeks.prep: Mirror, pencils, eraser, a picture of a face with proportion guidelines (search 'Loomis' or 'basic face proportions'). Keep an early-year sketch for comparison.
misconceptions: Drawing the eyes near the top of the head. Eyes are about halfway between the top of the head and the chin.
Drawing symbols (almond eyes, a 'nose triangle') instead of observing. Look in the mirror and draw shapes and values you actually see.

days.guide: Teach guidelines: oval; eyes halfway down; the face is about five eye-widths across; bottom of nose halfway from eyes to chin; mouth about one-third down from nose to chin; ears from eye line to nose line.

questions.q: Where are the eyes on the head?
questions.a: About halfway between the top of the skull and the chin.

questions.q: How far apart are the eyes?
questions.a: About one eye-width apart.

days.guide: Practice eyes, nose and mouth from the mirror, one page each.

questions.q: Why does the iris look partly covered by the upper eyelid?
questions.a: The upper lid naturally overlaps the top of the iris; showing the whole circle makes eyes look startled.

days.guide: Sketch the self-portrait lightly with guidelines.

questions.q: What is symmetry, and is a real face perfectly symmetrical?
questions.a: Symmetry is balance where both sides match; real faces are nearly but not perfectly symmetrical.

days.guide: Add value based on a single light source; shade eye sockets, under nose, under lower lip, neck.

questions.q: Which parts of the face usually fall into shadow with light from above?
questions.a: Eye sockets, under the nose, under the lower lip, under the chin and the neck.

days.guide: Compare with an earlier sketch and list improvements.

questions.q: Name one specific improvement.
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., eyes placed at the halfway line now.

weeks.assessment_key: Self-portrait rubric (1–4): proportions (eyes at halfway line, about one eye-width apart, nose bottom halfway between eyes and chin, mouth one-third from nose to chin, ears between eye and nose lines), observational detail, value showing a consistent light source, expression/personality. Proficient = proportions mostly correct and at least 4 values.

weeks.prep: 4–5 household objects of different heights and textures, a drawing paper, a paper viewfinder (rectangle cut from cardstock). An image of a Dutch Golden Age still life by Pieter Claesz.
misconceptions: Lining objects up in a row facing forward. Overlap objects and vary heights for depth and interest.
Placing the focal point dead center. Off-center (e.g., rule of thirds) is usually more dynamic.

days.guide: Arrange objects with overlap; make three thumbnails through the viewfinder.

questions.q: What is a focal point?
questions.a: The area that draws the viewer's eye first.

days.guide: Lightly draw the best thumbnail using sighting to check proportions (hold pencil at arm's length to compare sizes).

questions.q: How does overlap create depth?
questions.a: An object in front blocks part of the one behind, showing which is closer.

days.guide: Shade fully with a range of values and a consistent light source.

questions.q: Why include both very light and very dark values?
questions.a: Strong contrast makes objects look three-dimensional and creates emphasis.

days.guide: Analyze a Claesz still life (muted tones, strong light, objects arranged on a diagonal, symbols of transience). Compare to your composition.

questions.q: What message did many Dutch still lifes carry?
questions.a: Vanitas — the shortness of life and the passing nature of earthly pleasures, shown with objects like skulls, extinguished candles, watches or half-eaten food.

days.guide: Write the 150-word artist statement.

questions.q: What belongs in an artist statement?
questions.a: What the work is, materials, the choices you made and why, and what you want viewers to notice or feel.

weeks.assessment_key: Still life rubric (1–4 each): composition (overlap, varied sizes, clear off-center focal point, fills the page), proportion, value range (white to near black), craftsmanship. Artist statement (~150 words) proficient: names subject and medium, explains composition and value choices, connects to the Dutch still-life influence, reflects on challenge/success.

weeks.prep: Tempera or acrylic in red, yellow, blue, white and black; brushes; water cup; paper plate palette; paper towels; heavy paper with a pre-drawn 12-part wheel.
misconceptions: Thinking black is the only way to darken. Mixing a complement produces richer darks and neutrals.
Adding a lot of dark to light when mixing. Add dark to light in tiny amounts.

days.guide: Mix and paint the 12-part wheel from the three primaries only.

questions.q: Which primaries make green?
questions.a: Blue and yellow.

questions.q: Name the tertiary between red and violet.
questions.a: Red-violet.

days.guide: Paint tint scales (add white) and shade scales (add black) for two colors.

questions.q: What is a tint? A shade?
questions.a: Tint = a color plus white; shade = a color plus black.

days.guide: Paint four squares: complementary, analogous, monochromatic, triadic.

questions.q: What is the complement of blue?
questions.a: Orange.

questions.q: What is an analogous scheme?
questions.a: Colors next to each other on the wheel, such as blue, blue-green and green.

days.guide: Mix complements (red+green, blue+orange, yellow+violet) for browns and grays.

questions.q: Why do complements make neutral colors?
questions.a: Together they contain all three primaries, which cancel each other toward brown or gray.

days.guide: Label swatches and quiz yourself.

questions.q: What colors make up the triadic scheme of secondaries?
questions.a: Orange, green and violet.

weeks.assessment_key: Color wheel: 3 primaries (red, yellow, blue), 3 secondaries (orange, green, violet), 6 tertiaries (red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet) placed correctly. Schemes: complementary (opposites, e.g., blue/orange), analogous (3 neighbors, e.g., yellow, yellow-green, green), monochromatic (one hue with tints/shades), triadic (three equally spaced, e.g., red/yellow/blue or orange/green/violet). Quiz answers: primary can't be mixed; secondary = two primaries; tint = color + white; shade = color + black; tone = color + gray.

weeks.prep: Images of Van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889) and Picasso's The Old Guitarist (1903–04, Blue Period). Paints, sketchbook.
misconceptions: Thinking warm colors always mean happy and cool always sad. Context, value and brushwork also shape mood; cool can be calm or peaceful.
Choosing colors only for realism. Expressionist artists chose colors for feeling.

days.guide: Compare the two paintings: Starry Night uses swirling brushstrokes and contrasting yellow against blue for energy and emotion; The Old Guitarist uses mostly blue for sadness and isolation.

questions.q: How does Picasso use color to create mood in The Old Guitarist?
questions.a: Almost entirely blue (monochromatic, cool) to express sadness, poverty and loneliness.

questions.q: How do Van Gogh's brushstrokes add to the mood?
questions.a: Thick, swirling, rhythmic strokes create movement and intense emotion in the sky.

days.guide: Paint the same simple landscape twice: warm and cool.

questions.q: Name the warm colors and the cool colors.
questions.a: Warm: red, orange, yellow; cool: blue, green, violet.

days.guide: Choose a personal place and sketch three thumbnails.

questions.q: What is a thumbnail sketch?
questions.a: A small, quick sketch to plan composition.

days.guide: Write painting criteria.

questions.q: Give one criterion for a successful landscape.
questions.a: Example: clear foreground, middle ground and background to show depth.

days.guide: Discuss which thumbnail best meets the criteria.

questions.q: What is Expressionism?
questions.a: Art that uses distorted forms and bold colors to express emotions rather than realistic appearance.

weeks.assessment_key: Mood studies: two versions of the same landscape — one in warm colors (reds, oranges, yellows), one in cool (blues, greens, violets) — and a written sentence for each mood. Painting plan: three thumbnails and written criteria (color scheme, off-center focal point, foreground/middle/background for depth). Proficient: criteria are specific and the chosen thumbnail is justified by them.

weeks.prep: Paint, canvas board or heavy paper, brushes (large flat, medium, small round), the chosen thumbnail. Protect the work surface.
misconceptions: Painting distant hills as dark and detailed as nearby objects. Distant areas are lighter, cooler, less detailed (atmospheric perspective).
Starting with details. Block in big shapes first, then refine.

days.guide: Thin underpainting: block in the three grounds with diluted paint.

questions.q: Why start with an underpainting?
questions.a: It establishes composition and values and covers the white surface so colors relate better.

days.guide: Paint sky and distant areas lighter and cooler.

questions.q: What is atmospheric perspective?
questions.a: Distant objects appear lighter, bluer/cooler, less detailed and lower in contrast because of the air between viewer and object.

days.guide: Middle ground: more detail and saturation.

questions.q: What is the middle ground?
questions.a: The area between the foreground and background.

days.guide: Foreground: most detail, contrast and warm/strong color.

questions.q: Why put the most detail in the foreground?
questions.a: Nearby objects are seen most clearly, which makes them feel close.

days.guide: Add final details and sign.

questions.q: Where should you sign a painting?
questions.a: Usually in a lower corner, small and neatly.

weeks.assessment_key: Landscape progress rubric (1–4): clear foreground, middle ground and background; atmospheric perspective (background lighter, bluer, less detail); planned color scheme; focal point with most contrast/detail; craftsmanship (edges, brushwork). Proficient = all three grounds and visible atmospheric perspective.

weeks.prep: Finished painting. Image of a famous landscape (e.g., Hokusai, Monet's Impression, Sunrise, or Thomas Cole's The Oxbow). Clear a display area.
misconceptions: Jumping straight to 'I like it' or 'it's bad.' Feldman's method saves judgment for last.
Treating critique as only negative. Critique names strengths and specific improvements.

days.guide: Model Feldman's four steps on a famous landscape; your child completes each step.

questions.q: What are the four steps of Feldman's method?
questions.a: Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Judge.

questions.q: At which step do you give your opinion of quality?
questions.a: Judge — the last step.

days.guide: Critique own painting using personal and established criteria.

questions.q: What is the difference between personal and established criteria?
questions.a: Personal criteria are your own goals for the piece; established criteria are standards used in the art world (composition, technique, use of elements).

days.guide: Make one revision to strengthen the focal point (more contrast, detail or brighter color).

questions.q: Name two ways to emphasize a focal point.
questions.a: Increase contrast, add detail, use the brightest or complementary color, place it on a rule-of-thirds point, use leading lines.

days.guide: Write an artist statement for the painting.

questions.q: What place inspired your painting and how did you show its mood?
questions.a: Open answer — names the place and specific color/brushwork choices.

days.guide: Display drawings and painting; your child explains one choice in each.

questions.q: What did you learn from a family member's comment?
questions.a: Open answer.

weeks.assessment_key: Written critique rubric: Describe (subject, colors, objects — facts only), Analyze (elements and principles: color scheme, contrast, focal point, balance, depth), Interpret (meaning or mood with evidence), Judge (success with reasons based on criteria). Proficient: all four steps in order with evidence. Mini show: child explains one specific choice per work.

weeks.prep: Free musictheory.net lessons (Note Duration, Measures and Time Signatures), metronome app, bucket/hand drum and sticks or wooden spoons. Write 8 short rhythms.
misconceptions: Counting rests as silence without counting. Rests take up beats exactly like notes.
Thinking a dot adds one beat. A dot adds half the note's value (dotted half = 3 beats in 4/4).

days.guide: Complete the note-duration lesson; clap and count 8 rhythms aloud ('1, 2-and, 3, 4').

questions.q: In 4/4, how many beats does a half note get?
questions.a: 2 beats.

questions.q: How many eighth notes equal one half note?

days.guide: Identify meter in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 excerpts; conduct each pattern (2: down-up; 3: down-right-up; 4: down-left-right-up).

questions.q: What does the top number in a time signature tell you?
questions.a: How many beats are in each measure.

questions.q: What does the bottom number 4 mean?
questions.a: A quarter note gets one beat.

days.guide: Count sixteenths as 1-e-&-a, 2-e-&-a; clap patterns slowly with a metronome.

questions.q: How many sixteenth notes are in one quarter-note beat?

days.guide: Perform a 16-bar bucket rhythm with the metronome (start at 70 bpm).

questions.q: Why practice with a metronome?
questions.a: It keeps a steady beat and shows if you rush or drag.

days.guide: Take the rhythm quiz.

questions.q: How many beats does a dotted half note get in 4/4?
questions.a: 3 beats (2 + 1).

weeks.assessment_key: Rhythm quiz: in 4/4 whole note = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½, sixteenth = ¼, dotted half = 3, dotted quarter = 1½; rests equal matching notes. Meter identification: 2/4 = 2 quarter beats per measure, 3/4 = 3 (waltz), 4/4 = 4. Proficient: 80% on musictheory.net exercises. Performance: 16 bars steady with metronome, ≤2 errors = proficient.

weeks.prep: Keyboard (app or real piano), Chrome Music Lab, musictheory.net note-identification exercises.
misconceptions: Confusing treble and bass clef notes. Treble lines E-G-B-D-F, spaces F-A-C-E; bass lines G-B-D-F-A, spaces A-C-E-G.
Thinking every pair of neighboring white keys is a whole step. E–F and B–C are half steps (no black key between).

days.guide: Teach treble clef: lines Every Good Boy Does Fine, spaces F-A-C-E. Drill on musictheory.net.

questions.q: Name the treble clef lines from bottom to top.
questions.a: E, G, B, D, F.

questions.q: Name the treble clef spaces.
questions.a: F, A, C, E.

days.guide: Teach bass clef: lines Good Boys Do Fine Always, spaces All Cows Eat Grass. Drill.

questions.q: Name the bass clef spaces from bottom to top.
questions.a: A, C, E, G.

days.guide: Find C (left of two black keys), then play C, G and F major scales.

questions.q: Which black key is used in G major?
questions.a: F-sharp.

questions.q: Which black key is used in F major?
questions.a: B-flat.

days.guide: Build major scales using W-W-H-W-W-W-H; try D major.

questions.q: What is a half step?
questions.a: The distance from one key to the very next key (white or black).

questions.q: Build D major.
questions.a: D E F# G A B C# D.

days.guide: Take the note-reading and scale quiz.

questions.q: What are ledger lines?
questions.a: Short lines added above or below the staff for notes outside its range.

weeks.assessment_key: Note-reading quiz: name 10 treble and 10 bass notes (80% proficient). Scales: C major = C D E F G A B C (no sharps/flats); G major = G A B C D E F# G (one sharp); F major = F G A Bb C D E F (one flat). Major scale pattern: W-W-H-W-W-W-H.

weeks.prep: Find recordings: Gregorian chant, Hildegard von Bingen (e.g., 'O virtus Sapientiae'), a troubadour song, Palestrina's Missa Papae Marcelli (Kyrie), an English madrigal (e.g., Morley's 'Now Is the Month of Maying'), Japanese gagaku ('Etenraku') and kora music (e.g., Toumani Diabaté).
misconceptions: Thinking 'medieval' music is all the same. Chant is monophonic and sacred; Renaissance polyphony layers independent voices; secular songs were about love and daily life.
Calling chant 'harmony.' Chant is a single melody line (monophony), even with many singers.

days.guide: Listen to chant and Hildegard; describe melody (smooth, stepwise), texture (one line) and rhythm (free).

questions.q: What is monophony?
questions.a: A single melodic line with no accompaniment or harmony.

questions.q: Who was Hildegard von Bingen?
questions.a: A 12th-century German abbess, writer and composer of sacred music.

days.guide: Listen to Palestrina; raise a hand each time a new voice enters.

questions.q: What is polyphony?
questions.a: Two or more independent melodic lines sounding at the same time.

days.guide: Compare a troubadour song and a madrigal with sacred music.

questions.q: How is a madrigal different from chant?
questions.a: A madrigal is secular, polyphonic, in the everyday language and about topics like love; chant is sacred, monophonic and in Latin.

days.guide: Listen to gagaku and kora music and compare.

questions.q: What is the kora?
questions.a: A West African harp-lute with about 21 strings played by griots (storyteller-musicians).

questions.q: What is gagaku?
questions.a: Ancient Japanese imperial court music played by wind, string and percussion ensembles.

days.guide: Write the listening log on three pieces.

questions.q: Name one way all these traditions are similar.
questions.a: Example: music served religious or courtly purposes and was passed on by trained musicians/oral tradition.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening log rubric (1–4): for three pieces, names composer/tradition, time period, texture (monophony/polyphony), instruments or voices, language/purpose (sacred/secular), tempo/mood; compares using vocabulary. Key facts: Gregorian chant — monophonic, Latin, sacred, unaccompanied, free rhythm; Hildegard — 12th-century German abbess and composer; Palestrina — 16th-century Italian, polyphonic masses; madrigal — secular, polyphonic, vernacular (English/Italian) part-song; troubadours — medieval French poet-musicians singing of courtly love; gagaku — Japanese imperial court music; kora — 21-string harp-lute of West African griots.

weeks.prep: Recordings of Beethoven's Für Elise and Mozart's Twelve Variations on 'Ah vous dirai-je, Maman' (K. 265, the 'Twinkle' tune). Two different performances of one piece. Colored paper.
misconceptions: Thinking 'piano' means slow. Piano means soft; tempo terms (adagio, allegro) describe speed.
Thinking a variation is a new song. Each variation keeps the theme's structure but changes rhythm, harmony, texture or style.

days.guide: Teach Italian terms; mark them on a listening chart as the music plays.

questions.q: What does 'forte' mean?
questions.a: Loud.

questions.q: What does 'allegro' mean?
questions.a: Fast, lively.

days.guide: Map Für Elise with colored blocks: A (famous theme), B, A, C, A.

questions.q: What is rondo form?
questions.a: A recurring main theme (A) alternating with contrasting sections: A-B-A-C-A.

days.guide: Listen to several Mozart variations; describe the change in each (faster notes, minor key, melody in the left hand…).

questions.q: What famous tune is the theme of Mozart's variations?
questions.a: The melody known as 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' (also the ABC song).

days.guide: Compare two performances (tempo, dynamics, articulation).

questions.q: How can two performers make the same piece sound different?
questions.a: By choosing different tempos, dynamics, articulation (staccato/legato) and phrasing.

days.guide: Give the form and expression quiz.

questions.q: What is the difference between staccato and legato?
questions.a: Staccato is short and detached; legato is smooth and connected.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: dynamics pp (pianissimo, very soft), p (piano, soft), mp (mezzo piano), mf (mezzo forte), f (forte, loud), ff (fortissimo, very loud), crescendo (gradually louder), decrescendo/diminuendo (gradually softer); tempo largo (very slow), adagio (slow), andante (walking), moderato (moderate), allegro (fast), presto (very fast); articulation staccato (short, detached), legato (smooth, connected). Für Elise form: rondo A-B-A-C-A. Theme and variations: a theme followed by altered versions.

weeks.prep: Keyboard or ukulele, Chrome Music Lab 'Chords,' a 12-bar blues recording (e.g., 'Johnny B. Goode' or a classic blues), chords for 'This Land Is Your Land' (in C: C, F, G).
misconceptions: Thinking major means loud and minor means soft. Major/minor describe the third of the chord (bright vs darker sound), not volume.
Building triads by playing every other key including black keys randomly. A triad stacks every other note of the scale: root, 3rd, 5th.

days.guide: Build C, F and G triads by stacking every other note.

questions.q: What notes are in a C major triad?
questions.a: C, E, G.

questions.q: What notes are in a G major triad?
questions.a: G, B, D.

days.guide: Play major and minor triads (C vs Cm: C-E♭-G); describe the sound.

questions.q: What changes between C major and C minor?
questions.a: The middle note (the 3rd) is lowered a half step: E becomes E-flat.

days.guide: Play I-IV-V-I in C; listen for the changes in a 12-bar blues.

questions.q: What are I, IV and V in the key of G?
questions.a: G, C and D.

questions.q: Write the 12-bar blues pattern.
questions.a: I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I.

days.guide: Strum or play C, F, G to 'This Land Is Your Land.'

questions.q: What is harmony?
questions.a: Two or more notes sounding together, such as chords supporting a melody.

days.guide: Give the chord quiz by ear and on paper.

questions.q: Spell an A minor triad.
questions.a: A, C, E.

weeks.assessment_key: Chord quiz key: C major = C-E-G; F major = F-A-C; G major = G-B-D; A minor = A-C-E; D minor = D-F-A; E minor = E-G-B. Major triad = root + major 3rd (4 half steps) + perfect 5th (7 half steps); minor = root + minor 3rd (3 half steps) + perfect 5th. In C major: I = C, IV = F, V = G. 12-bar blues: I-I-I-I / IV-IV-I-I / V-IV-I-I. By-ear: identify major (bright) vs minor (darker) — 80% proficient. Play-along: changes on time with steady strum.

weeks.prep: Ukulele (tuned G-C-E-A) or keyboard, chord charts for C, Am, F, G, metronome, practice log, two songs chosen with your child (one major, one minor/different tempo).
misconceptions: Stopping the strum to change chords. Keep the strumming hand moving; lift fingers a little early.
Practicing only the parts you already know. Isolate the hard chord change and loop it slowly.

days.guide: Teach D-D-U-U-D-U strum on C and Am (count 1, 2-&, -&, 4-&... or 'down, down-up, up-down-up').

questions.q: Write the strum pattern.
questions.a: Down, down, up, up, down, up (D-D-U-U-D-U).

days.guide: Practice C-Am-F-G changes at 60 bpm, one chord per measure.

questions.q: Name the chords in this progression as Roman numerals in C major.
questions.a: C = I, Am = vi, F = IV, G = V.

days.guide: Learn the verse of the first song.

questions.q: What is a 'pivot finger'?
questions.a: A finger that stays down or moves least between chords to make changes easier.

days.guide: Learn a contrasting song.

questions.q: How does the contrasting song differ?
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., minor key sounds darker, slower tempo.

days.guide: Record, listen and set practice goals.

questions.q: Write a specific practice goal.
questions.a: Example: 'Switch F to G cleanly 10 times in a row at 70 bpm by Friday.'

weeks.assessment_key: Recording and log rubric (1–4): steady strum pattern, clean chords (no buzzing), chord changes on time at a set tempo, practice log with daily minutes and specific goals (e.g., 'C to F at 70 bpm'). Proficient: plays both song sections with a steady beat and ≤3 stumbles.

weeks.prep: Chrome Music Lab Song Maker (free) and/or MuseScore. Set the key to C major.
misconceptions: Writing random notes without repetition. Unity comes from repeating and developing a motif.
Ending on any note. Ending on the tonic (C in C major) sounds finished.

days.guide: Create three 2-bar motifs in Song Maker; choose the strongest.

questions.q: What is a motif?
questions.a: A short musical idea that repeats and develops through a piece.

days.guide: Extend into a 4-bar question (ends unresolved) and 4-bar answer (ends resolved).

questions.q: What is a phrase?
questions.a: A musical 'sentence,' often 4 bars long, ending with a cadence.

days.guide: End on the tonic; compare with ending on other notes.

questions.q: What is a cadence?
questions.a: The ending of a phrase that gives a sense of rest or pause.

questions.q: What is the tonic in C major?
questions.a: C.

days.guide: Notate the 8-bar melody in MuseScore with rhythm and dynamics.

questions.q: In 4/4, does a bar of half note + quarter note + two eighths add up?
questions.a: Yes: 2 + 1 + ½ + ½ = 4 beats.

days.guide: Evaluate for unity (repetition) and variety (change); revise a bar.

questions.q: Why does music need both unity and variety?
questions.a: Unity makes it hold together; variety keeps it interesting.

weeks.assessment_key: 8-bar melody rubric (1–4): clear motif that repeats/varies, question phrase (bars 1–4, ending on a non-tonic note such as G/D) and answer phrase (bars 5–8, ending on tonic), mostly stepwise with some leaps, correct notation (measures add up), dynamics marked. Proficient: 4 measures of 4 beats each per phrase, ends on tonic, shows unity and variety.

weeks.prep: MuseScore or Song Maker, keyboard/ukulele, the 8-bar melody from week 16, criteria checklist.
misconceptions: Making the B section too similar to A. Contrast in key, rhythm, register or mood.
Picking chords that clash with the melody. Choose the chord (I, IV or V) that contains the melody's main note in each bar.

days.guide: Add chords: for each bar choose I (C-E-G), IV (F-A-C) or V (G-B-D) containing the melody's main notes.

questions.q: A bar's melody uses mostly F and A. Which chord fits?
questions.a: IV (F major: F-A-C).

days.guide: Compose an 8-bar B section with contrast.

questions.q: What is ABA form?
questions.a: A section, contrasting B section, then A returns.

days.guide: Add a rhythm part or bass line (roots of chords).

questions.q: What is an accompaniment?
questions.a: Music that supports the melody, such as chords, bass line or rhythm.

days.guide: Rehearse the composition and two songs with a checklist.

questions.q: Name two items on a performance checklist.
questions.a: Steady tempo, correct notes/chords, dynamics, posture, confident start and ending.

days.guide: Play for a family member and record feedback.

questions.q: What feedback will you act on?
questions.a: Open answer.

weeks.assessment_key: ABA composition rubric (1–4): A section 8 bars with I-IV-V harmony matching melody notes, contrasting 8-bar B section, return of A, added rhythm or bass part, notation readable. Feedback recorded and one revision planned. Proficient: clear ABA with harmony that fits most bars.

weeks.prep: Instrument, paper for programs, phone to record. Set a recital time for family.
misconceptions: Stopping after a mistake. Keep the beat going and recover.
Rushing because of nerves. Breathe and count in before starting.

days.guide: Run the full program twice; isolate and fix problem spots.

questions.q: How do you fix a problem spot?
questions.a: Practice that measure slowly, loop it, then add the measures before and after.

days.guide: Design the program with titles and program notes.

questions.q: What are program notes?
questions.a: Short descriptions helping the audience understand each piece.

days.guide: Perform two contrasting songs and the original composition.

questions.q: What is stage presence?
questions.a: Confidence and connection with the audience — posture, introductions, eye contact, bowing.

days.guide: Watch the recording and evaluate with the rubric.

questions.q: Name one strength and one area to improve from the recording.
questions.a: Open answer tied to rubric.

days.guide: Write a reflection on growth this semester.

questions.q: What new skill can you do now that you couldn't in September?
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., read bass clef, play chord changes.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (1–4): accuracy (notes/chords), steady tempo, expression (dynamics, contrast between songs), stage presence (introduces pieces, bows, recovers from mistakes). Self-evaluation proficient: uses rubric with evidence from the recording and names a next goal. Program includes titles, composers and short program notes.

weeks.prep: Compass, ruler, pencil, colored pencils, images of the Alhambra (Granada, Spain) tilework and mosque tiles (Smarthistory). Watch a short tutorial on constructing an 8-point star.
misconceptions: Thinking Islamic art never shows figures anywhere. Religious spaces generally avoid figures, so geometric, vegetal (arabesque) and calligraphic designs dominate, but figurative art appears in some secular manuscripts.
Freehanding the pattern. Accurate construction uses compass and straightedge.

days.guide: View Alhambra tilework and mosque tiles; discuss why geometry, arabesque and calligraphy are central.

questions.q: Why are geometric patterns important in Islamic art?
questions.a: Religious art generally avoids depicting living beings, so geometry, plant forms and calligraphy are used; endless repeating patterns suggest the infinite nature of God and unity.

questions.q: Where is the Alhambra?
questions.a: Granada, Spain — built by the Nasrid rulers in the 13th–14th centuries.

days.guide: Construct an 8-point star: draw a circle, divide it into 8 with diameters, connect points to make two overlapping squares.

questions.q: How many degrees apart are the 8 division lines?

days.guide: Repeat the star motif on a grid so tiles connect.

questions.q: What is a tessellation?
questions.a: A pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps or overlaps.

days.guide: Color with a planned scheme, keeping symmetry.

questions.q: What kind of symmetry does an 8-point star have?
questions.a: Radial (rotational) symmetry — and 8 lines of reflection.

days.guide: Write the reflection.

questions.q: What is an arabesque?
questions.a: A flowing, interlacing design based on vines, leaves and plant forms.

weeks.assessment_key: Pattern artwork rubric (1–4): accurate 8-point star construction (circle divided into 8 equal parts, two overlapping squares), repeats into a tiled grid, symmetry and tessellation, planned color scheme applied consistently, neat craftsmanship. Reflection proficient: explains that geometric patterns express ideas of unity, order and infinity in Islamic art and are used in mosques where figurative imagery is avoided.

weeks.prep: Foam printing plates (or flat erasers), dull pencil, water-based block ink, brayer, a tray, paper. Image of Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c. 1831).
misconceptions: Forgetting prints are reversed. Letters and directional images must be drawn backwards on the plate.
Using too much ink. Roll a thin, even layer that makes a soft hissing sound.

days.guide: Design a print with bold shapes and positive/negative space, inspired by Hokusai.

questions.q: What is negative space?
questions.a: The empty space around and between the subject.

days.guide: Transfer the design to foam and press lines in (incise) with a dull pencil.

questions.q: Will a word on your plate print correctly?
questions.a: No — it will print backwards unless you carve it reversed.

days.guide: Ink with a brayer and pull test prints; adjust pressure.

questions.q: What is a brayer?
questions.a: A small hand roller used to spread ink evenly.

days.guide: Pull 4 prints; sign and number them.

questions.q: What does '3/4' on a print mean?
questions.a: This is the third print in an edition of 4.

days.guide: Compare your process to The Great Wave.

questions.q: In relief printing, do the carved-away areas print?
questions.a: No — the raised surface takes ink; carved (incised) areas stay the paper color.

weeks.assessment_key: Edition rubric (1–4): strong positive/negative space design, clear incised lines, consistent inking, 4 matching prints, each signed and numbered in pencil below the image (1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 left, title center, signature right). Reflection proficient: explains that Hokusai's print was made by a team — the artist drew the design, a carver cut it into multiple woodblocks (one per color), a printer inked and printed, and a publisher sold many copies — unlike your single-person foam process.

weeks.prep: Chisel-tip calligraphy marker, gold marker or metallic paint, guide-lined paper. Images of the Book of Kells (c. 800, Insular Gospel book, Trinity College Dublin) and a Persian manuscript page (e.g., the Shahnameh of Shah Tahmasp, 16th century).
misconceptions: Holding the chisel tip at random angles. Keep a consistent pen angle (about 30–45°) for even thick-thin strokes.
Thinking illumination means just colorful. Illuminated manuscripts are decorated with gold or silver that literally 'lights up' the page.

days.guide: Compare the Book of Kells and a Persian manuscript page.

questions.q: What is the Book of Kells?
questions.a: An illuminated Latin manuscript of the four Gospels made by Irish/Scottish monks around 800 CE.

questions.q: What material were medieval manuscripts written on?
questions.a: Vellum or parchment (prepared animal skin).

days.guide: Practice an italic or gothic alphabet with a chisel marker at a steady angle.

questions.q: What is calligraphy?
questions.a: Decorative, skilled handwriting.

days.guide: Design an illuminated initial with border decoration.

questions.q: Why were initials decorated?
questions.a: To mark the start of important sections and to glorify the text.

days.guide: Write a short quote in calligraphy; add metallic accents.

questions.q: What does 'illumination' refer to?
questions.a: Decoration with gold or silver (and bright colors) that makes the page shine.

days.guide: Compare preservation then and now.

questions.q: How does digitizing manuscripts help?
questions.a: It lets anyone view them online while the fragile originals are protected from light and handling.

weeks.assessment_key: Illuminated page rubric (1–4): consistent calligraphic hand (gothic or italic) with even spacing and pen angle, decorated initial with border motifs, metallic accents, layout balance. Manuscript comparison: Book of Kells — Christian Gospels, Celtic knots, interlace, animals, Latin script; Persian manuscript — poetry/epic, detailed figures and landscapes, floral borders, Persian script. Preservation: then — vellum, bindings, monastery libraries, copying by scribes; now — climate control, limited light, digitization for online access.

weeks.prep: Images of an Aztec codex (e.g., Codex Borbonicus or Codex Mendoza) and adinkra symbol chart. Potatoes or foam, plastic knife (adult supervision), fabric or paper, paint/ink.
misconceptions: Copying sacred or cultural symbols without understanding them. Learn meanings, credit the culture, and create your own personal symbol.
Thinking codices are read like European books. Many Mesoamerican codices are read with pictographs, often screenfold, and some read in zigzag patterns.

days.guide: Analyze codex images: bold outlines, flat bright colors, figures in profile, glyphs for dates/names telling stories.

questions.q: What is a codex?
questions.a: A handmade book; Aztec codices used pictures and glyphs on bark paper or deerskin, often folded like a screen.

questions.q: What kind of information did Aztec codices record?
questions.a: History, calendars, religious rituals, tribute lists and genealogies.

days.guide: Learn 8 adinkra symbols and their meanings (see key).

questions.q: Where do adinkra symbols come from?
questions.a: The Akan people of Ghana (and Côte d'Ivoire).

questions.q: What does Sankofa mean?
questions.a: 'Go back and get it' — learn from the past.

days.guide: Design a personal symbol; carve a potato or foam stamp (adult cuts if needed).

questions.q: Why must stamp designs be simple?
questions.a: Fine details don't carve or print clearly; bold shapes print best.

days.guide: Stamp a repeating pattern on fabric/paper.

questions.q: Name two kinds of repeating patterns.
questions.a: Grid (straight rows), half-drop, alternating, rotated.

days.guide: Write about respectful inspiration vs copying.

questions.q: Give one way to be respectful when inspired by another culture's art.
questions.a: Learn the meaning and history, credit the source, avoid sacred items used out of context, and make original work.

weeks.assessment_key: Stamped textile rubric (1–4): repeating pattern (grid, alternating or rotated), includes a personal symbol and at least one adinkra symbol with written meaning, consistent printing. Adinkra meanings (Akan, Ghana): Gye Nyame — 'except God' (supremacy of God); Sankofa — 'go back and get it' (learn from the past); Dwennimmen — ram's horns (humility and strength); Akoma — heart (patience, love); Adinkrahene — chief of symbols (greatness, leadership); Funtunfunefu — Siamese crocodiles (unity, democracy); Eban — fence (safety, love, security); Ese ne tekrema — teeth and tongue (friendship, interdependence). Reflection proficient: distinguishes respectful inspiration (research, credit, understanding meaning, creating original work) from copying/appropriation.

weeks.prep: Open space, prompt cards (characters, settings, objectives). Know Magna Carta context (1215, King John and barons at Runnymede).
misconceptions: Blocking a scene partner's idea ('No, that's not a dragon'). In improv, accept offers and build: 'Yes, and…'
Thinking a tableau is just standing still. Use levels, facial expressions and focus to tell a story.

days.guide: Warm up: tongue twisters ('Red leather, yellow leather'), stretches, mirror exercise.

questions.q: Why do actors warm up?
questions.a: To prepare voice and body, improve diction and focus, and build ensemble trust.

days.guide: Play 'Yes, and' story building, one sentence each.

questions.q: What does 'Yes, and' mean in improv?
questions.a: Accept your partner's idea and add to it.

days.guide: Create frozen tableaux of historical moments like King John sealing Magna Carta.

questions.q: What is a tableau?
questions.a: A frozen stage picture showing a moment with bodies, levels and expressions.

questions.q: What happened at the Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.a: English barons forced King John to agree to a charter limiting royal power at Runnymede.

days.guide: Improvise scenes where each character has an objective and an obstacle.

questions.q: What is an objective?
questions.a: What a character wants in the scene.

days.guide: Journal on which game built confidence.

questions.q: What is an ensemble?
questions.a: A group of performers working together as a team.

weeks.assessment_key: Participation checklist (yes/no): warms up fully, accepts and builds on offers, makes clear choices, uses levels in tableaux, plays a clear objective, supports partners. Journal proficient: names a game, describes a specific moment, explains how it built confidence.

weeks.prep: Monologue excerpts from A Midsummer Night's Dream (e.g., Puck's 'If we shadows have offended,' Helena's 'How happy some o'er other some can be,' or Bottom waking from his dream). Read and choose one with your child.
misconceptions: Thinking projection means shouting. Projection uses breath support from the diaphragm to carry the voice without strain.
Confusing stage left with audience left. Stage directions are from the actor's view facing the audience.

days.guide: Practice belly breathing and projecting lines across a room.

questions.q: What is projection?
questions.a: Making your voice carry to the back of the audience using breath support.

days.guide: Say 'I can't believe you did that' ten ways (angry, proud, sarcastic…).

questions.q: What is inflection?
questions.a: The rise and fall of pitch in the voice that changes meaning or emotion.

days.guide: Walk as five characters (king, old man, nervous kid, villain, athlete), changing posture, tempo and center (head, chest, hips).

questions.q: How can posture show character?
questions.a: A king stands tall and slow; a nervous person hunches and moves quickly.

days.guide: Teach stage areas; call out blocking commands ('Cross downstage left').

questions.q: If you move toward the audience, which direction are you moving?
questions.a: Downstage.

questions.q: What is blocking?
questions.a: The planned movements and positions of actors on stage.

days.guide: Perform a 1-minute monologue from A Midsummer Night's Dream.

questions.q: In 'If we shadows have offended,' who is speaking and to whom?
questions.a: Puck, speaking to the audience at the end of the play, suggesting it was all a dream.

weeks.assessment_key: Monologue rubric (1–4): memorization, projection, diction, vocal variety (inflection, pace, pauses), physical choices and focus. Stage directions: upstage = away from audience, downstage = toward audience, stage right/left = actor's right/left facing the audience; 9 areas (UR, UC, UL, R, C, L, DR, DC, DL). Proficient: clear and audible throughout with meaning conveyed.

weeks.prep: Script of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 5, Scene 1) or another public-domain one-act. Read it first. Household materials for design sketches.
misconceptions: Thinking subtext is the same as the lines. Subtext is what the character really thinks or wants under the words.
Assuming Shakespeare's plays used elaborate sets. Elizabethan public theatres had little scenery; words, costumes and props set the scene.

days.guide: Read the scene aloud together; summarize plot and characters.

questions.q: Why is the mechanicals' 'tragedy' funny?
questions.a: They are amateur actors who overact, explain everything literally (a man plays the Wall), forget lines and mangle words, turning a sad story into comedy.

questions.q: Who plays Pyramus?
questions.a: Nick Bottom, the weaver.

days.guide: Research original staging (Globe-era open-air theatre, daylight, male actors for all roles, little scenery).

questions.q: Who played women's roles in Shakespeare's time?
questions.a: Boys or young men; women were not allowed on the public stage in England.

days.guide: Write a character profile with objective and subtext.

questions.q: What is subtext?
questions.a: The unspoken thoughts and motives beneath a character's lines.

days.guide: Sketch set, costume and prop designs from household materials.

questions.q: How could you show the 'Wall' character simply?
questions.a: An actor holding cardboard painted like bricks, with fingers making the chink.

days.guide: Compare comic patterns with a sitcom (misunderstanding, physical comedy, characters unaware they're funny).

questions.q: Name one comic technique shared with sitcoms.
questions.a: Dramatic irony, slapstick physical comedy, exaggeration, a 'show within a show,' running gags.

weeks.assessment_key: Character profile rubric: name, role, relationships, traits with line evidence, objective, obstacles, subtext for 2 lines, voice/movement choices. Design sketches: set, costume and prop sketches labeled with materials and reasons. Key facts for Pyramus and Thisbe: performed by the 'rude mechanicals' for Theseus's wedding; Bottom plays Pyramus, Flute plays Thisbe, Snout plays Wall, Starveling plays Moonshine, Snug plays Lion, Quince speaks the Prologue; the lovers talk through a chink in a Wall, plan to meet at Ninus' tomb, Thisbe flees a Lion leaving her bloody mantle, Pyramus thinks she's dead and kills himself, Thisbe finds him and kills herself — a tragic story performed so badly it's comic.

weeks.prep: Script copies, pencil, props and costumes from the design plan, family actors, phone for sound effects.
misconceptions: Memorizing lines without cue lines. Learn the line before yours so you know when to speak.
Saving blocking notes in your head. Write them in pencil in the script.

days.guide: Hold a read-through with family playing roles.

questions.q: What is a read-through?
questions.a: The first rehearsal where the cast reads the script aloud together.

days.guide: Block the scene; write notes like 'X DSL' (cross downstage left).

questions.q: What does 'cheat out' mean?
questions.a: Turn your body partly toward the audience so they can see your face.

days.guide: Drill cue lines.

questions.q: What does 'off-book' mean?
questions.a: Having lines memorized without the script.

days.guide: Run the full scene with props; give notes.

questions.q: What is a run-through?
questions.a: Performing the whole scene/play without stopping.

days.guide: Add costumes, sound or lighting cues; run again.

questions.q: What is a cue?
questions.a: A signal (line, action or sound) for an actor or technician to do something.

weeks.assessment_key: Rehearsal journal (each day): what was rehearsed, director's notes received, personal goal, progress. Proficient: 5 entries with specific notes (e.g., 'Cheat out downstage on the death speech') and evidence of being off-book by day 4.

weeks.prep: Set a performance time, audience seating. Find a filmed production (e.g., a filmed Shakespeare, National Theatre at Home, or a local theater show).
misconceptions: Writing a review that only summarizes the plot. Reviews evaluate acting, design and directing with evidence.
Breaking character when something goes wrong. Stay in the moment and keep going.

days.guide: Hold a full dress rehearsal with costumes and props.

questions.q: Why is a dress rehearsal important?
questions.a: It's the final full run with all elements, catching problems before the audience sees it.

days.guide: Perform the play for family or group; take a curtain call.

questions.q: What is a curtain call?
questions.a: When actors bow at the end of a performance.

days.guide: Watch a filmed or live production, taking notes.

questions.q: Name one design element to note.
questions.a: Set, costumes, lighting, sound, makeup, props.

days.guide: Write a review with evidence.

questions.q: Give an example of evidence in a review.
questions.a: Example: 'When the lights shifted to blue during the forest scene, the mood became dreamlike.'

days.guide: Reflect on own performance.

questions.q: What choice are you proudest of?
questions.a: Open answer with a specific moment.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (1–4): memorization, projection/diction, characterization, blocking, ensemble work. Review rubric: introduces the production, evaluates acting, design (set, costume, lighting, sound) and directing with specific examples, and gives an overall judgment with reasons. Self-reflection: names choices made and their effect.

weeks.prep: Phone or camera. Image of Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936, Nipomo, California) and a modern advertisement.
misconceptions: Centering every subject. The rule of thirds places subjects along lines/intersections for more dynamic images.
Thinking photos are always objective. Photographers choose framing, angle and moment, shaping the message.

days.guide: Analyze Migrant Mother (close framing, worried expression, children turned away, made for the Farm Security Administration during the Great Depression) and an ad.

questions.q: What was the purpose of 'Migrant Mother'?
questions.a: To document poverty of migrant farm workers during the Great Depression and build support for government aid.

questions.q: How does an ad use composition to influence viewers?
questions.a: It places the product at the focal point, uses lighting, angles and attractive models to make it desirable.

days.guide: Take 10 photos with the rule of thirds (turn on grid lines).

questions.q: What is the rule of thirds?
questions.a: Dividing the frame into a 3×3 grid and placing key subjects along the lines or at intersections.

days.guide: Take 10 photos with leading lines and natural frames.

questions.q: What are leading lines?
questions.a: Lines in the image (roads, fences, rivers) that guide the eye to the subject.

days.guide: Photograph one object from 5 angles.

questions.q: What effect does a worm's-eye view have?
questions.a: Shooting from below makes the subject look large, powerful or imposing.

days.guide: Select and caption best 5.

questions.q: What is depth of field?
questions.a: How much of the photo, front to back, is in sharp focus.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo portfolio of 5 (1–4): each photo clearly shows a named technique (rule of thirds, leading lines, framing, angle, depth of field), is in focus and well exposed, and has a caption. Proficient: 5 strong photos showing at least 4 different techniques.

weeks.prep: Camera, free photo editor (e.g., Snapseed, Photos app, GIMP). Read a short explainer of Creative Commons licenses.
misconceptions: Thinking anything online is free to use. Most images are copyrighted; use your own, public domain or Creative Commons images with attribution.
Photographing people without asking. Ask permission, especially of children and before sharing online.

days.guide: Plan a 6–8 photo story with a shot list (wide establishing, medium, close-up details).

questions.q: What is a photo essay?
questions.a: A series of photos that together tell a story or explore a theme.

days.guide: Shoot, asking permission before photographing people.

questions.q: Why ask permission before photographing people?
questions.a: It respects their privacy and consent, especially before sharing.

days.guide: Crop and adjust exposure.

questions.q: What does 'exposure' mean?
questions.a: How light or dark the photo is, based on the light reaching the sensor.

days.guide: Teach copyright (automatic for creators), Creative Commons (creator lets others use with conditions like attribution) and consent; write sharing rules.

questions.q: What does 'CC BY' mean?
questions.a: Creative Commons Attribution — you may use the work if you credit the creator.

questions.q: Is a photo you found on Google free to use?
questions.a: Not necessarily — it's usually copyrighted unless marked public domain or licensed for reuse.

days.guide: Present as a captioned slideshow.

questions.q: What story does your essay tell?
questions.a: Open answer.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo essay rubric (1–4): 6–8 photos telling a story with beginning, middle and end; variety of shots (wide, medium, close-up); captions; editing improves without distorting; permission obtained for people. Sharing rules include consent, privacy (no addresses/faces of kids without permission), credit and a license choice.

weeks.prep: Clay or LEGO, a free stop-motion app (e.g., Stop Motion Studio), phone stand, storyboard template. Find a clip of Wallace & Gromit or a classic stop-motion short.
misconceptions: Moving characters too much between frames. Small moves create smooth motion.
Shooting near a window. Changing daylight causes flicker; use steady lamp light.

days.guide: Watch stop-motion clips; discuss how still frames create motion (persistence of vision).

questions.q: How does stop-motion create the illusion of movement?
questions.a: Many still photos, each with a tiny change, play quickly in sequence so the brain sees continuous motion.

days.guide: Make a 2-second ball bounce at 12 fps.

questions.q: How many frames do you need for 2 seconds at 12 fps?
questions.a: 24 frames.

questions.q: Why are frames closer together at the top of the bounce?
questions.a: The ball slows down at the top, so it moves less between frames.

days.guide: Storyboard a 30-second story.

questions.q: How many frames for 30 seconds at 12 fps?
questions.a: 360 frames.

days.guide: Build characters from clay or LEGO.

questions.q: Why add a wire armature to clay characters?
questions.a: It supports the figure and holds poses between frames.

days.guide: Build a set and plan lighting.

questions.q: What causes flicker in stop-motion?
questions.a: Changing light (sunlight, shadows) or camera exposure between frames.

weeks.assessment_key: Test animation: ball bounce of about 24 frames (2 s × 12 fps) with spacing showing slow at top, fast near bottom and squash on impact. Storyboard rubric: 6–9 panels with beginning, middle, end; camera angle and action notes; estimated frames (30 s × 12 fps = 360 frames).

weeks.prep: Stop-motion app, tripod or stack of books, the storyboard, characters and set. Original composition from week 17 for soundtrack (optional).
misconceptions: Bumping the camera mid-scene. Secure the camera; use a remote or timer.
Using copyrighted songs. Use original or royalty-free music.

days.guide: Shoot scene 1 following the storyboard.

questions.q: What is a frame rate?
questions.a: The number of frames shown per second (e.g., 12 fps).

days.guide: Shoot scenes 2–3.

questions.q: How can you make a character look like it's jumping?
questions.a: Raise it slightly each frame using clear wire or support, then lower it back down.

days.guide: Edit timing; add titles and credits.

questions.q: What belongs in credits?
questions.a: Names of people and their roles, and music/sound sources.

days.guide: Add soundtrack or effects.

questions.q: Why use your own music?
questions.a: It's original and avoids copyright problems.

days.guide: Premiere the film; reflect on production roles.

questions.q: Which production role did you enjoy most, and why?
questions.a: Open answer.

weeks.assessment_key: Stop-motion film rubric (1–4): story (clear beginning, middle, end), animation quality (smooth movement, stable camera, consistent lighting), editing (timing, titles, credits), sound (soundtrack/effects synced). Reflection names roles (director, animator, set designer, editor, sound designer) and what was learned.

weeks.prep: Air-dry clay, aluminum foil, wire, clay tools (toothpicks, forks). Images of Donatello's David (bronze, c. 1440s) and Michelangelo's David (marble, 1501–1504) from several angles.
misconceptions: Building thick, solid clay forms. Use a foil armature so the clay is thinner and dries without cracking.
Only making the front interesting. Sculpture in the round should work from every view.

days.guide: Compare the two Davids from multiple viewpoints.

questions.q: Which David was carved from marble and which was cast in bronze?
questions.a: Michelangelo's is marble (carved); Donatello's is bronze (cast).

questions.q: What moment does Michelangelo's David show?
questions.a: The moment before the fight with Goliath — tense and focused.

days.guide: Build a foil and wire armature.

questions.q: What is an armature?
questions.a: An internal support framework for a sculpture.

days.guide: Add clay over the armature, building major forms.

questions.q: Is adding clay additive or subtractive sculpture?
questions.a: Additive.

days.guide: Add texture and details with tools.

questions.q: What does 'in the round' mean?
questions.a: A freestanding sculpture meant to be viewed from all sides.

days.guide: Smooth; let dry; sketch from three views.

questions.q: What is contrapposto?
questions.a: A pose with weight on one leg so hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions, looking natural and relaxed.

weeks.assessment_key: Sculpture progress rubric (1–4): stable armature, forms built additively over armature, texture and details, works in the round; three-view sketches (front, side, back). Comparison key: Donatello's David — bronze, smaller, youthful, wearing a hat and boots, standing over Goliath's head after victory, relaxed contrapposto; Michelangelo's David — marble, about 17 ft tall, muscular, shown before the battle with focused, tense expression and sling over the shoulder, carved (subtractive).

weeks.prep: Bar of soap (Ivory carves well), plastic knife, paper clip/toothpick for detail, paint and sealer (Mod Podge or clear acrylic) for the clay piece.
misconceptions: Carving details too early. Remove big chunks first, then refine.
Carving thin projections that break. Keep forms compact.

days.guide: Sketch the design from front, side and top.

questions.q: Why sketch three views before carving?
questions.a: So you know how the form looks from all sides before removing material.

days.guide: Rough-carve the soap, removing big chunks.

questions.q: Is soap carving additive or subtractive?
questions.a: Subtractive — material is removed.

days.guide: Refine details and smooth surfaces.

questions.q: Why can't you easily fix a mistake in subtractive sculpture?
questions.a: Material once removed can't be added back.

days.guide: Paint and seal the clay sculpture.

questions.q: What is a patina?
questions.a: A surface finish or coloring, like the green on aged bronze, or a painted imitation.

days.guide: Write an artist statement for one sculpture.

questions.q: Compare your carving process to Michelangelo's.
questions.a: Both are subtractive — removing material to reveal the form; he carved marble with chisels, you carved soap with a plastic knife.

weeks.assessment_key: Soap carving rubric (1–4): planned from three views, recognizable compact form, smooth surfaces, details refined. Clay finish: painted thoughtfully, sealed. Artist statement: subject, method (additive vs subtractive), choices, challenges, connection to studied sculptors.

weeks.prep: All the year's artwork, poster board, cardstock, glue, boxes for pedestals. Google Arts & Culture account-free virtual tour (e.g., the Uffizi or the Met).
misconceptions: Including everything. Curating means selecting the best and most representative works.
Labels that only give a title. Museum labels include title, date, medium, size and a short interpretive text.

days.guide: Take a virtual tour; note how works are spaced, grouped and labeled.

questions.q: What does a curator do?
questions.a: Selects, organizes and presents artworks for an exhibition and writes interpretive information.

days.guide: Select 8–10 works representing each unit.

questions.q: Why choose works from every unit?
questions.a: To show the range of skills and growth across the year.

days.guide: Mat 2-D work and make pedestals for sculptures.

questions.q: What is a mat?
questions.a: A border (usually cardboard) around a 2-D artwork that frames and protects it.

days.guide: Write museum-style labels.

questions.q: What goes on a museum label?
questions.a: Artist name, title, date, medium, dimensions, and a short description.

days.guide: Plan the exhibition layout.

questions.q: How might you group works?
questions.a: By unit, medium, theme or chronology.

weeks.assessment_key: Curated portfolio rubric (1–4): 8–10 works representing every unit, mounted/matted neatly, museum labels (artist, title, date, medium, dimensions, 2–3 sentence description), logical layout plan. Proficient: all units represented and labels complete.

weeks.prep: Exhibition space, hooks/tape, the song, monologue and animation file, response cards, invitations to family/friends.
misconceptions: Hanging work too high. Hang 2-D art with the center at about eye level (around 57–60 inches).
Thinking only museums give art value. Context changes how art is viewed, but meaning comes from the work and its audience.

days.guide: Install the exhibition.

questions.q: At about what height should the center of a framed artwork hang?
questions.a: Eye level — about 57–60 inches from the floor.

days.guide: Rehearse song, monologue and gallery talk.

questions.q: What is a gallery talk?
questions.a: A short talk explaining artworks to visitors.

days.guide: Host the showcase.

questions.q: Which work got the strongest reaction and why?
questions.a: Open answer.

days.guide: Collect visitor response cards.

questions.q: What makes feedback useful?
questions.a: It is specific about what worked and what could change.

days.guide: Reflect on home vs museum viewing.

questions.q: How can location change how people value art?
questions.a: A museum setting suggests importance and expertise; home settings feel personal; lighting and labels affect attention.

weeks.assessment_key: Showcase rubric: exhibition installed neatly with labels; performances of a song, monologue and animation screening; gallery talk explains at least 3 works with vocabulary. Reflection proficient: compares home vs museum viewing (lighting, labels, scale, crowds, prestige, cost) and how location affects perceived value.

weeks.prep: Sketchbook, portfolio, camera/phone, slideshow app. Ideas for a summer sketchbook challenge (e.g., one drawing a day, 30-day prompts).
misconceptions: Measuring growth only by realism. Growth includes ideas, risk-taking, process and confidence.
Goals that are too vague. Make them specific and measurable.

days.guide: Compare first and last drawings; list three improved skills.

questions.q: Which skill improved most? Show evidence.
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., value range from 3 to 9 tones.

days.guide: Photograph all work; build a digital portfolio slideshow.

questions.q: Why photograph art in even, indirect light?
questions.a: To avoid glare and shadows and show true colors.

days.guide: Create one free-choice artwork.

questions.q: Which elements and principles did you use?
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., complementary colors and emphasis.

days.guide: Write a letter to your future self about your artistic identity.

questions.q: What is artistic identity?
questions.a: The interests, styles, subjects and values that make your art your own.

days.guide: Set goals for VAPA 8 and choose a summer challenge.

questions.q: Write a SMART art goal.
questions.a: Example: 'Fill 30 sketchbook pages with observational drawings by August 31.'

weeks.assessment_key: Digital portfolio rubric: photos of all major works, organized by unit, with titles and short reflections. Reflection letter proficient: names favorite medium and why, describes 3 skills that improved with evidence, describes artistic identity (style, interests) and goals for next year.
